strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem: exploiting slot annotations to improve task-oriented utterance embeddings without intent-pair supervision. The combination of template augmentation, template learning, and utterance–template contrastive learning is well motivated, and Figures 2–4 make the pipeline understandable.

The reported results are encouraging across five intent-classification benchmarks. In Table 2, TaDSE with MLP achieves 83.87 average accuracy versus 81.82 for DSE. Including baselines adapted to the augmented data helps assess whether gains extend beyond additional training data.

The component ablations provide useful evidence. For example, Table 4 shows SNIPS improving from 93.29 with augmentation to 95.29 with template loss and 96.14 with pairwise loss. The automatically extracted slots on CLINC150 and the reported compression failures also provide informative evidence about the method’s limitations.
weaknesses: The evaluation protocol remains insufficiently precise for a clear Findings recommendation. Appendix C’s reference to the 'full utterance/template training set representations' does not establish whether the nearest-neighbor index contains original utterances, synthetic utterances, templates, or combinations, and whether comparable systems use identical reference sets. Index composition can affect accuracy independently of encoder quality. Specify the reference banks, label assignment for shared templates, and exact training/development splits.

Important implementation details are missing or ambiguous: contrastive temperatures, optimizer, pooling and MLP architecture, and normalization during compression. Equations 1–2 include unperturbed self-representations in their denominators rather than clearly specifying the dropout-view candidates used by SimCSE. Moreover, augmentation creates multiple utterances sharing a template, yet Equation 3 treats all off-diagonal utterances as negatives without describing how shared-template cases are handled. These ambiguities matter particularly because executable artifacts are only promised upon acceptance.

The manuscript provides no repeated-run variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests despite claiming significant improvements. Several compression gains correspond to only a few test examples. Model selection also needs clarification: Appendix D uses test-set learning curves to motivate additional training for the MLP variant, while validation-based selection is explicitly described only for the compression coefficient. Report uncertainty and establish that all configuration choices were made independently of test performance.

The semantic-compression analysis supports an exploratory interpretation, but does not establish the claimed measure of semantic well-formedness. Before renormalization, interpolation toward a shared template mechanically contracts distances between utterances sharing that template. Consequently, improved alignment and worsened uniformity can arise from the transformation itself. Explicit normalization and suitable interpolation or shuffled-anchor controls are needed. Table 5’s mixed results and t-SNE visualizations do not independently validate the stronger interpretation.

The supervision assumptions and scope of the claims need tighter qualification. Four datasets supply gold slot annotations, so 'unsupervised' applies to intent supervision rather than the complete pipeline; annotation-cost advantages are not measured. The source of inference-time templates for compression should also be explicit. Finally, the main comparison emphasizes older embedding baselines, while the newer commercial comparison covers only two datasets. These experiments support a narrower contribution to in-domain intent retrieval than the broader state-of-the-art dialogue-embedding claims.
